source_refs.note: Limitations: a main subheading of 28.4 Gas Chromatography, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 181-183.

items: GC works only for volatile (easily vaporised) substances.
Samples must be thermally stable. Compounds that decompose at high temperatures cannot be used.
Large biomolecules like proteins and polymers cannot be analysed by GC because they do not vaporise easily.
Instruments and maintenance costs for GC are high.

blocks.text: An impure sample of lactic acid, CH₃CH(OH)COOH contains butanone as the only contamination. The mixture is analysed using gas chromatography. Butanone is found to have a longer retention time than lactic acid.
book_errors: longer retention time than lactic acid

blocks.prompt: i) Suggest suitable substances that could be used as the mobile and stationary phases.
blocks.explanation: Mobile phase: an inert carrier gas such as helium or nitrogen. Stationary phase: a non-volatile liquid of high boiling point (such as a long-chain hydrocarbon) coated on particles of silica or alumina.

blocks.prompt: ii) Describe how the percentage composition of the mixture can be determined from the gas chromatogram.
blocks.explanation: First identify the peaks by their retention times. Measure the area of each peak (½ × base × height). Percentage of butanone = area of the butanone peak ÷ (sum of the areas of both peaks) × 100; the percentage of lactic acid is found in the same way.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Butanone has the shorter retention time, not the longer one. GC separates mainly by volatility: butanone boils at about 80 °C, while lactic acid, with an –OH and a –COOH group and strong hydrogen bonding, is far more polar and boils at about 220 °C (with decomposition). Lactic acid therefore stays longer in the column and comes out after butanone. The rule that non-polar substances move more slowly on a non-polar column only decides the order of compounds of similar volatility.
